Some students referred to the information that an arresting officer is required to give to the person they are arresting (s28) and then speculated that such information must have been provided here, concluding that the arrest was therefore lawful. If this was offered rather than the second qualifying requirement (PACE s24(5)(c)(iii)) the maximum mark awarded was 4.
71623b-jun24-q-08:
This question directed students’ attention to Article 2 of the ECHR and asked them to advise the police as to whether they might be liable under s6 HRA due to their shooting dead of Brice. Most students seemed well-prepared for this question and there were many thorough and perceptive answers to it.

S6 HRA states that it is unlawful for a public authority to act incompatibly with a Convention right. The police, as state agents, are a public authority and so bound to uphold the rights in the ECHR, including the right to life under Article 2.

A majority of students recognised the police as being bound to uphold Convention rights under s6 HRA, and were able to explain the scope of Article 2(1) as imposing a negative duty not to take life, and a positive duty to protect life. Many identified that the negative duty not to take life was relevant given that the police had killed Brice; some also pointed out that the positive duty to protect life was relevant given that Callie and Duke were both in danger.

Most students were aware of the circumstances, set out in Article 2(2), in which it may be lawful to take life, and identified the exception relevant to the scenario as deprivation of life in defence of another person from unlawful violence. Callie and Duke had already been violently beaten by Brice and what the police saw when they arrived was Brice pointing a gun at Duke’s head, whilst shouting, ‘He’s dead.’ The police did not know the gun was a fake, so they believed there to be a real and immediate risk to Duke’s life.

With regard to the police’s mistaken belief that the gun was real, many students referred to cases such as McCann v UK and Armani da Silva v UK, holding that the police could rely on a mistaken belief provided that it was honest or genuine and based on subjectively good reasons, that the force used was necessary. Applying this to the facts in the scenario, it could be argued that the officer who fired the shot that killed Brice did have such a belief. Callie and Duke had been violently beaten and dragged into the garden – their injuries and distress would have been clearly visible to the officer. Brice was pointing what looked to be a real gun at Duke, threatening to kill him, so it would have appeared to the officer that there was a real and immediate risk to life.

When fatal force is used, Article 2.2 states that it must be no more than absolutely necessary. Many students concluded that in the circumstance described above, firing a fatal shot was no more force than absolutely necessary in defence of Duke.

The failure of the call handler to pass on information to the police attending the incident was dealt with in a variety of ways. Some students saw it as a failure in operational planning, often referring to the requirement for effective planning highlighted in Finogenov v Russia. Some argued that the call handler’s failure could therefore result in the police being in breach of Article 2 (assuming the call handler was a member of the police). A minority of students misread the scenario and thought that the call handler knew the gun was a fake and had not passed this information on, whereas what was known, but not communicated, was that Brice had not fired the gun. Perceptive answers pointed out that the call handler’s failure to pass on the information that the gun had not been fired did not detract from the clear and obvious threat to life the police were presented with (a realistic gun pointed at someone’s head), meaning their use of lethal force against Brice would probably be justified under Article 2.2.
71623b-jun24-q-09:
This question had two areas of content: a 10-mark part requiring an examination of the concept of justice, and a 5-mark part discussing the extent to which remedies available for a breach of human rights might achieve justice. Most students attempted both parts, and most divided their time appropriately between the two.

An examination of the meaning of justice could initially involve offering synonyms and / or explanations of what justice might entail – eg. fairness, equal treatment, impartial decision making. To develop the examination of the concept of justice, some philosophical theories of justice could be explored, evaluated, and perhaps linked to aspects of our current legal system. Different types of justice (eg. corrective justice, procedural justice, or substantive justice) might be explained, and again relevant aspects of the English legal system examined to show the presence or lack of a particular type of justice.

Theories of justice often explained in answers included those of Aristotle, Bentham, Marx, Rawls and Nozick. Some stronger answers linked the theory to an aspect of the English legal system or to a case, and sometimes evaluated the theory – for example, pointing out the potential injustice to minorities if a utilitarian approach to justice was taken. Different types of justice, such as procedural, corrective, distributive, and substantive, were often identified. Illustrative examples were wide-ranging, including how cuts to legal aid might be seen to undermine procedural justice, or how a sentence or an award of damages might achieve corrective justice. Some explanations of distributive justice were vague and failed to address the different ways in which a ‘just’ distribution might be achieved – eg. based on merit or need.

A wide variety of approaches were adopted in response to the second part of this question, on the extent to which remedies available for a breach of human rights might achieve justice. Most students identified an award of damages as a remedy for a breach of human rights; some anchored this with reference to s8 of the Human Rights Act 1998 (HRA) and a few pointed out that S8 does not guarantee a remedy. Many discussed the adequacy or inadequacy of financial compensation, sometimes linking this to the facts of a case, or more generally to a breach of Article 2, pointing out that no monetary award can fully compensate for the loss of a life. Many also referred to the right to compensation in Article 5.5. Some also considered how the remedy of an injunction might achieve justice – for example, by prohibiting the publication of private information. A few students referred to a declaration of incompatibility under s4 HRA as promoting justice, in that it creates pressure for a change in law and so resulting legislation could ensure justice in the future.
71623b-jun24-q-10:
This question concerned incidents that occurred during a march and a demonstration. Students were asked to consider two things. First, the rights and remedies of Gerson (the march organiser), Halima (a marcher), and other demonstrators as a consequence of the incidents. Second, whether any subsequent convictions for public order offences might be challenged. The main areas of law raised by this scenario were policing powers in relation to marches and assemblies under the Public Order Act 1986 (POA) and the ECHR rights to freedom of association (Article 11) and freedom of expression (Article 10).

A useful starting point taken by some students was to distinguish between a procession (the march) and an assembly (the static demonstration that followed). Gerson had organised a procession and so under s11 POA had a duty to give the police six days’ advance notice of this, including its date, time, proposed route, and his name and address. Since he failed to do this, he had committed an offence under s11(7) POA.

Most students were aware of s11 and were able to set out with varying degrees of accuracy the details required in the notice. Only some, however, pointed out that Gerson’s failure to give advance notice meant that he had committed an offence under the POA. (This offence was relevant to the second part of the question, asking whether convictions for public order offences might be challenged.)

Halima was arrested for ignoring police instructions about the route to take. S12 allows a senior police officer to impose conditions on a march / procession. The officer must reasonably believe the march may result in serious public disorder, serious damage to property, or serious disruption to the life of the community. The power is to impose such conditions as appear necessary to prevent the disorder, damage, or disruption, including the power to vary the route.

Answers varied in the accuracy with which s12 was explained and applied. Stronger responses set out both the power to impose conditions under s12 and the grounds for imposing them. This law could then be applied to the scenario, pointing out that the police had imposed a condition as to the route of the march, and considering the ground(s) on which it might have been imposed. In weaker responses, the police power to impose conditions was sometimes merely mentioned and often not linked to any source of law. The grounds permitting the imposing of a condition tended not to be set out. And there was often little or no application of s12, so the instructions given by the police in the scenario, regarding the route of the march, were not identified as an exercise of this power.

It is an offence for a person taking part in a march / procession to fail to follow a condition imposed by the police (s12(5) POA). So, Halima had committed an offence when she ignored the condition regarding the route. Better answers identified this behaviour as an offence, which could then be considered when addressing the second part of the question regarding the challenging of convictions. Weaker answers sometimes asserted that Halima had a right to ignore the police instructions regarding the route.

The domestic law most obviously relevant to the static demonstration at the factory gates was s14 POA, and the common law rules on breach of the peace. Under s14, the grounds for imposing conditions on assemblies are the same as those for processions. In the scenario, a condition was imposed limiting the duration of the assembly to 45 minutes. Given the scuffles between demonstrators and police, and the threat of violence breaking out between the demonstrators and the factory workers, the ground for imposing this condition was likely to be a reasonable belief that it was necessary to prevent serious public disorder.

Again, what distinguished stronger answers from weaker ones was the level of accuracy in explaining s14, and whether or not it was applied to the scenario.

Some students dealt with the ending of the demonstration after 45 minutes as an exercise of the power to ban under s13 POA. Some credit was given for this, but s13 relates to banning a procession, ie. a march, not a static assembly.

Another approach adopted by some students was to identify the demonstration as a trespassory assembly, which could be prohibited under s14A POA. This was certainly creditworthy, depending on the accuracy of the law and application in the answer. The definition of a trespassory assembly in s14A refers to it taking place on land to which the public has no or only limited access. Some students argued that the demonstrators had no right to be at the factory gates or to block them. S14A also requires a reasonable belief that the assembly will result either in serious disruption to the life of the community or significant damage to land or a building of historical, architectural, archaeological, or scientific importance. Students who applied s14A well-tended to argue that the police would have reasonably believed that there would be serious disruption to the life of the community (it was less likely that the factory building, or gates were of architectural or historical importance). Weaker answers sometimes merely mentioned banning an assembly with no reference to a relevant source of law.

Gerson chaining himself to the gates, the scuffles between demonstrators and the police, and the threat of violence to demonstrators from the factory employees could all have been dealt with as actual or threatened breaches of the peace. Many students showed at least some knowledge of this area of law, with better answers defining a breach of the peace (often citing the R v Howell definition) and then applying it to the scenario. Given the scuffles between the demonstrators surrounding Gerson and the police, there was an imminent threat of harm being done. Stronger answers referred to common law powers to take reasonable steps, including arrest, to prevent an imminent breach of the peace and then applied this to the cutting free and arrest of Gerson. Some perceptive answers questioned whether the arrest of the demonstrators was a reasonable step given that the threat of violence was coming from the factory employees.

Aggravated trespass, although not required, was another creditworthy approach to Gerson chaining himself to the factory gates. S68 of the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994 defines this offence as requiring trespass and behaviour intended to intimidate, obstruct or disrupt a lawful activity. Students who knew the definition of aggravated trespass usually argued that there might be a trespass by Gerson when he attached himself to the factory gates, and then that this behaviour was disrupting the workers who were lawfully trying to get into the factory. Weaker answers tended just to mention aggravated trespass without defining or applying it.

A minority of students applied the relatively new offence of locking-on (s1 Public Order Act 2023) to Gerson chaining himself to the gates. Again, this was not required but was certainly relevant and creditworthy. The offence is committed when a person attaches themselves to land (as Gerson did) and doing so causes serious disruption to two or more people or to an organisation. Since Gerson was obstructing factory workers from entering it would seem that the main elements of the offence were present.

Some students also referred to the public order offences found in ss 1-5 POA. And again, this was creditworthy but not required. It should be noted that knowledge of these offences is not part of the Human Rights component of the Specification and maximum marks can always be obtained without including them. The public order offences that are referred to in the second part of the question are those within the Specification and engaged by the facts of the scenario – ie. the offences discussed above in relation to failure to give notice of a procession under s11, and failure to comply with a condition imposed under s12 or s14, as well as breach of the peace.

Articles 10 and 11 were engaged in the scenario, since protestors were exercising their right to freedom of expression by criticising the agricultural practices encouraged by Full Range Foods, and their right to freedom of assembly and association when marching and demonstrating. Most students recognised the relevance of Article 11, but not all mentioned Article 10. It was possible to reach the top of the good band if only Article 11 was considered, and to reach the excellent band if Article 10 was dealt with more briefly, with Article 11 considered in more depth and detail. Many students referred to the police being agents of the State and so bound to uphold ECHR rights under s6 HRA.

Most answers elaborated on the scope of Article 11 and pointed out that it protects peaceful protest even if the demonstration annoys or offends those opposed to it. Stronger answers explained some of the relevant law relating to counter protest (eg. Platform ‘Artze fur das Leben’ v Austria) pointing out that the police have a positive duty to facilitate a peaceful protest and that this may require policing to allow both the protest and a counter protest. Some students pointed to the police accompanying the initial march as an example of them fulfilling this positive duty. And some identified a potential interference with the Article 11 right when the police failed to take measures to deal with the factory employees who were

threatening violence against the demonstrators. This was a perceptive point: the original demonstration was peaceful, at least initially; arguably the threat of violence came, not from the demonstrators the police arrested, but from the factory workers, who the police took no action against.

Students who referred to Article 10 usually started by explaining its scope. Many referred to freedom of expression extending to ideas that offend, shock or disturb (often citing Handyside v UK). This could be applied to the views of the demonstrators that might offend or disturb Full Range Foods or its employees but would nevertheless fall within the scope of Article 10.

A majority of answers recognised the qualified nature of the rights protected by Articles 10 and 11, but the degree of accuracy in the explanation and application of 10.2 and 11.2 varied. An area of improvement from last year was recognising that the phrase ‘prescribed by law’ required any interference to have a clear legal basis in domestic law. Stronger responses pointed to specific rules of domestic law such as s12 and s14 POA, and the common law relating to breach of the peace as meeting this requirement.

Most students who addressed 10.2 and 11.2 were able to list legitimate aims for an interference and to identify an aim relevant to the scenario, such as the prevention of disorder and crime.

But, as noted in the Introduction, fewer students could explain and apply the requirement for an interference to be ‘necessary in a democratic society’. When this was handled well, students typically explained that in order for an interference to be lawful it had to correspond to a pressing social need (Sunday Times v UK) and to be proportionate to a legitimate aim. Some students pointed out that proportionality required a fair balance to be struck between the aim and the right (Kudrevicius v Lithunia). Others explained proportionality as requiring the measure to be the least restrictive option.

The imposing of a condition regarding the route of the march was generally perceived as a proportionate interference, since it allowed the march to continue. Similarly, Halima’s arrest was generally regarded as proportionate, since she was ignoring a condition imposed to facilitate a peaceful, safe protest. And the arrest of one individual might be seen as a proportionate measure to ensure the route was respected, thus facilitating the peaceful protest. It was therefore unlikely she would be able to challenge her conviction under s7 HRA.

There were differing views on Gerson’s arrest for breach of the peace. Some saw it as a proportionate interference with Gerson’s rights under Article 10 and 11, arguing that he was blocking access to the factory and provoking violence from the workers. Others considered Gerson’s arrest to be disproportionate, arguing that one person chained to the gates did not block access, and that the threat of violence was coming, not from Gerson, but from the factory employees. On this view, Gerson could challenge his conviction (perhaps by appeal or by seeking judicial review) and be awarded damages for the breach to his article 10 and 11 rights under s8 HRA.

The arrest of other demonstrators for breach of the peace was generally argued to be a disproportionate interference with their article 10 and 11 rights, since those arrested were being threatened with violence by the employees and were themselves peaceful. Students who reached this conclusion argued the demonstrators could challenge their convictions and seek a remedy under s8 HRA.

Stronger answers: • Demonstrated accurate knowledge of domestic law, in particular s12 and s14 POA, and breach of the peace

• Applied this law to the facts of the scenario • Identified the offences committed by Gerson and Halima • Explained the scope of Articles 11 and 10, and why they were engaged • Explained the provisions of 11.2 and 10.2 • Recognised that ‘prescribed by law’ required a legal basis in UK law for an interference and linked this to the POA and breach of the peace powers • Explained the meaning of ‘necessary in a democratic society’ and considered the proportionality of the measures taken by the police • Reached a conclusion as to whether convictions could be challenged.

Weaker answers: • Made only vague, inaccurate, or superficial reference to domestic law • Did not systematically apply law to the facts of the scenario • Did not identify the offences committed by Gerson and Halima • Did not explain the provisions of 11.2 and 10.2 • Did not apply 11.2 or 10.2 • Did not reach clear conclusions regarding whether convictions could be challenged.
71623b-jun24-q-11:
The scenario-based part of this question involved two incidents: the searching of Jane by a police officer, Karin, and the subsequent detention of Jane in the police station for two hours.

The first incident concerned the police power to stop and search under ss1-3 PACE and the right to a private life under Article 8.

Under ss1 PACE a police officer has power to stop and search a person for stolen or prohibited items provided that the officer has reasonable grounds to believe that person has stolen or prohibited items on them. S2 sets out information that the officer must provide to the person about to be searched (the officer’s name and the police station to which they are attached; the object of the search; the officer’s grounds for conducting it). S3 requires a record to be made of the search (recording the object of the search, the grounds for making it, the date, time and place) and a copy of this record to be given to the person searched.

Stronger answers identified the relevant source of law, set out the above provisions accurately, then applied them to the scenario. They discussed the objective nature of ‘reasonable grounds’, often explaining this as requiring a belief based on intelligence or on behaviour and doubting the sufficiency of Jane’s previous convictions or of her proximity to a pharmacy as reasonable grounds to search her for stolen items. (Credit was given for the alternative view that there were reasonable grounds to believe Jane had stolen items on her.) While knowledge of Code of Practice A is not required, a number of answers did refer to this when elaborating on the meaning of reasonable grounds to stop and search.

There was confusion in some answers between the grounds for stop and search in ss1-3 PACE, and those for arrest under s24 PACE - eg. stating that the police officer had power to stop and search if they had reasonable grounds to believe the person had committed a crime. Under ss1-3 PACE a police officer can stop and search a suspect without reasonable suspicion that they have committed or are about to commit a crime. What is required is reasonable grounds to believe that stolen or prohibited items will be found. So, a police officer who has reasonable grounds to suspect that a person is in innocent possession

of a stolen or prohibited article may stop and search the person even though there would be no power of arrest.

Weaker responses were vague about the law governing stop and search, or sometimes made no reference at all to PACE. Some students mentioned the so-called suspicion-less power to stop and search under s60 of the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994, but often with little idea of the difference between this power and the one under ss1-3PACE. As s60 was not raised by the facts of the scenario, students were certainly not required to deal with it, but credit was given when it was dealt with accurately.

Since Article 8 protects both physical integrity (Wainwright v UK) and private information, such as medical records (M.S. v Sweden) it was clearly engaged by Karin’s search of Jane. Many students recognised that Karin, as a police officer, was an agent of the State and so bound by the ECHR. Most students who recognised the relevance of Article 8 were able to explain its scope and to identify medical information and correspondence as private.

Article 8(2) allows for lawful interference with private life provided that such interference is in accordance with law and necessary in a democratic society for one of the listed aims.

Students varied in their ability to explain and apply Article 8 (2): some did not mention it at all; others set it out, but only applied part of it, often identifying the prevention of crime as a legitimate aim but going no further than that. Stronger answers, however, explained that the phrase ‘in accordance with law’ referred to the need for a legal basis for any interference with private life, and then linked this to the stop and search provisions in PACE. (If the stop and search had not been based on reasonable grounds then logically it was not in accordance with law.)

To illustrate law that might interfere with private life, some students referred to the State’s power to intercept communications under the Investigatory Powers Act 2016 and to the protection given to private information under the Data Protection Act 2018. Whilst detailed knowledge of such legislation is certainly not required by the Specification, awareness of it was creditworthy as illustrative of what might constitute a legal interference with private life.

The requirement for an interference to be ‘necessary in a democratic society’ presented more of a challenge, as explained in the Introduction above. Stronger answers recognised that this required the interference to be proportionate to the aim of preventing crime and explained that this meant using the least intrusive means possible. Since the letter Karin read was from Jane’s doctor and had no relevance at all to any crime, most students who addressed this issue argued that reading it was clearly unnecessary and disproportionate. Karin therefore appeared to have breached Jane’s Article 8 rights, giving rise to a right of action under ss 6 and 7, and to a remedy under s8 HRA.

Some answers dealt only with stop and search powers under UK law, and others only with Article 8. When just one of these was dealt with, an answer could be placed in the ‘good’ band depending on the standard of the explanation and application.

The second incident concerned Jane’s detention at the police station. This raised both Article 5 and English law on arrest (s24 PACE). Almost all students recognised that Article 5 was engaged here, but answers varied as to how accurately the provisions of this article were set out.

A useful approach was to start by explaining that for Article 5 to be engaged a deprivation of liberty was required, and to distinguish a deprivation of liberty from a mere restriction of movement. Cases such as Guzzardi v Italy were often used to explore the meaning of a deprivation of liberty, with reference to the degree or intensity of the restraint, and to factors such as the type, duration, effects and manner of implementation of the measure. Applying this to Jane, we were told that she was ‘reluctant’ to go to the police station and was ‘taken’ there by Karin. So, she seemed to have been taken against her will, and did not seem to have been free to leave for two hours, leading many students to conclude that she had been deprived of her liberty.

Alternatively, some students drew an interesting analogy with Austin v UK, in which the kettling of the demonstrators for seven hours had not been deemed to be a deprivation of liberty, and so argued that detaining Jane for two hours was probably not sufficient to constitute such a deprivation. Credit was given for both approaches, but, as some students perceptively pointed out, the decision in Austin relied on the purpose of the kettle having been to isolate and contain a large crowd, in volatile and dangerous conditions. The police were regarded as having had no alternative but to impose an absolute cordon in order to avert a risk of serious injury or damage. Therefore, the imposition of the cordon in Austin was deemed the least intrusive and most effective means to maintain order and protect the public. The facts of the scenario were very different however: the purpose of taking Jane to the police station was merely to try to identify suspects on CCTV. A number of students pointed out that this could have been done at a different time, or by showing the footage to other people – ie. there were other, less intrusive ways to achieve this. Many students were aware that there is no legal obligation to answer a police officer’s questions, nor to help in their inquiries. So, if Jane had been forced to go to the police station, this pointed to a deprivation of liberty.

If Jane had been deprived of her liberty, then the question arose as to whether one of the permitted limitations set out in Article 5.1 (a) to (c) applied. The most obviously relevant limitation was 5.1 (c): lawful arrest in order to bring the person before the competent legal authority on reasonable suspicion of them having committed an offence, or when reasonably considered necessary to prevent them fleeing having done so.

The English law on arrest is set out in PACE. S24 requires reasonable grounds to suspect the person arrested has committed or is about to commit an offence, and reasonable grounds to believe the arrest is necessary for one of the listed purposes in s24(5). Most students who addressed this had no difficulty in arguing that Karin did not have reasonable grounds to suspect Jane of involvement in the burglaries, given that her search of Jane had yielded no evidence. They then concluded that the arrest was unlawful, and that Jane would be entitled to compensation under Article 5.5.

Some students argued that since Jane had only been detained for two hours her detention was lawful, since under PACE the police can detain a suspect for 24 hours before charge. But this 24- hour period relates to the time between arrest and charge. If Jane had been lawfully arrested, then she could be held for 24 hours before being charged. But, as argued above, it was unlikely that her arrest was lawful (because there were no reasonable grounds to suspect her of committing a crime) and, if it was not, then the police were in breach of Article 5 in detaining her.

The third part of Q11 is on non-substantive law and carries 7 marks. This year it required students to assess the role of the judge in the trial of the two suspected burglars. This relates to the part of the Specification referring to ‘The judiciary: types of judges. Role of judges … in criminal courts (human rights)’. So what students were expected to discuss was the general nature of the judge’s role in conducting a criminal trial: dealing with admissibility of evidence, instructing the jury on the law,

summing up for the jury at the end of the trial before they retire, passing sentence if the defendant is found guilty, keeping order in court, and ensuring the trial is fair and that both sides have a fair opportunity to present their case.

It should be noted that this part of the question did not require any discussion of the offence of burglary, which is not in the Specification.

Performance on this aspect of Q11 varied. Some students handled it very well, concisely setting out some or all of the aspects of a judge’s role listed above. Some were able to elaborate on particular aspects of the role – eg. consideration of aggravating and mitigating factors in determining sentence. Others, though, struggled to identify any role beyond sentencing, and some confused the role of a judge in a civil trial with that of one in a criminal trial.

Some students also considered the role of the judge if the case were to be heard in a Magistrates’ Court and were given credit for this.

Stronger answers: • Dealt with Article 8 as well as PACE in relation to the letter and the body search • Explained and applied the PACE provisions permitting stop and search • Distinguished between a deprivation of liberty and a restriction of movement in relation to Article 5 • Used the factors from Guzzardi v Italy to reach a conclusion as to whether Jane had suffered a deprivation of liberty • Explained and applied the requirement for reasonable grounds for arrest • Reached a reasoned conclusion regarding breach of A8 and A5 • Included remedies • Were able to use law from cases cited • Explained key aspects of the role of a judge in a criminal trial. Weaker answers: • Did not reference relevant provisions from PACE at all, or did so only in a vague or inaccurate way • Did not demonstrate understanding of the objective nature of the requirement for reasonable grounds in relation to the PACE provisions on stop and search and on arrest • Did not explain deprivation of liberty and / or did not consider whether there had been a deprivation of liberty engaging Article 5 • Failed to apply the law or did so only in a superficial manner • Did not include the role of the judge, or demonstrated a lack of understanding about the role, sometimes confusing it with a judge’s role in a civil case • Struggled to identify any other role of the judge beyond sentencing.
71623b-jun25-q-01:
The correct answer was option C:

‘The right to life under Article 2 also gives everyone a right to die.’

This option was chosen by 77% of students, showing most were aware of case law from the ECtHR holding that Article 2 does not grant a right to die.

The most commonly chosen incorrect answer was option D: ‘The right to respect for private and family life under Article 8 could be breached by environmental pollution.’ This is true because in several cases, failure by the State to provide information about environmental risks has been held to breach Article 8, e.g. Guerra v Italy.
71623b-jun25-q-02:
The correct answer was option C:

‘Both individuals and States may bring actions in the European Court of Human Rights.’

This option was chosen by 39% of students. The most commonly chosen incorrect answer was option B: ‘A judge must not apply an English law statute if it is incompatible with the ECHR.’ This was an understandable mistake, as students will have learned that courts are public authorities under s6 of the Human Rights Act 1998, which states that a public authority must not act incompatibly with the ECHR. But under the doctrine of parliamentary sovereignty, parliament is the supreme law-making power, and courts must apply acts of parliament. If a superior court considers an act to be incompatible with the ECHR it can make a declaration of incompatibility under s4 of the Human Rights Act 1998, but it cannot strike down or invalidate the statute.
71623b-jun25-q-03:
The correct answer was option D:

‘To set out rules for a local area.’

This option was chosen by 70% of students. Given that the majority of students answered this question correctly, it was perhaps a little surprising to see some confusion in question 6 between statutory instruments and by-laws.

Incorrect answers were mostly distributed between option A (‘To add detail to existing legislation’) and option C (‘To make law in time of emergency’). Option A relates to statutory instruments and option C to orders in council (which are generally statutory instruments, too).
71623b-jun25-q-04:
The correct answer was option C:

‘Judges’ pay is determined by government.’

This option was chosen by 41% of students. It is false because protection of judges’ pay from political interference is a way of protecting judicial independence. In the UK, judges’ pay is set by an independent body (the Senior Salaries Review Body) which advises the government. It is paid from the Consolidated Fund and so not subject to annual parliamentary budgets.

The most common incorrect answer was option B: ‘Judges can review the legality of a government decision.’ This was incorrect as judges can review the legality of a government decision through judicial review.
71623b-jun25-q-05:
The correct answer was option C:

‘The burden of proof in a criminal trial is usually on the prosecution.’

This option was chosen by 62% of students.

Incorrect answers were mostly distributed between options B (‘Criminal prosecutions are usually brought by the victim’) and D (‘The standard of proof in a civil trial is beyond reasonable doubt’). Option B was incorrect because criminal prosecutions are usually brought by the State. Option D was incorrect because the standard of proof in a civil trial is on the balance of probabilities.
71623b-jun25-q-06:
This question required students to explain how statutory instruments are made and to give two examples of matters that might be dealt with using a statutory instrument. If no examples were given, the maximum marks available was 3, so essentially there were 3 marks for the initial explanation and 2 for the examples.

 Recognising that statutory instruments are a form of delegated legislation was an obvious place to start and many students did this. The explanation could then be developed by outlining how the delegation of power occurs (Parliament delegates law-making power by means of a parent or enabling act) and then identifying who the power is delegated to (in the case of statutory instruments the delegation is to a government minister). These three points were enough to merit 3 marks. Other creditworthy points relevant to how statutory instruments are made were explanations of affirmative and /or negative resolution procedures.

Examples could have been general or specific. General examples relate to the nature/purpose of a statutory instrument – e.g. to add detail to primary legislation; to modify primary legislation; to set commencement dates for provisions in primary legislation; to deal with emergencies (e.g. Orders in Council are a type of statutory instrument). Specific examples relate to a particular statutory instrument or (some part of) its content. A combination of general and specific could be regarded as two examples – e.g. statutory instruments can deal with supplying detail to supplement primary legislation (general), and an example of a statutory instrument that does this (specific), e.g. Construction and Use Regulations for Road Vehicles to supply detail for primary legislation on Road Traffic.

Some students were clearly well-prepared for this question, and wrote confident, concise answers gaining good marks. Other students struggled to identify what a statutory instrument was. There was a lot of confusion with statutory interpretation (an understandable guess) and

some confusion with by-laws (also understandable as both are types of delegated legislation). Some answers showed knowledge of what a statutory instrument was, but not of how it was made, while others discussed the value of statutory instruments (e.g. to save parliamentary time) straying away from the focus of the question.
71623b-jun25-q-07:
Students were asked to suggest why the stopping and searching of Amanda would have been unlawful under s1 of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 (PACE). It was helpful to start by explaining the law. PACE s1(1) makes it clear that the stop and search power applies to a person in a public place (not a dwelling). The power is to stop and search for stolen or prohibited items (e.g. an offensive weapon) PACE s1(2), provided the officer has reasonable grounds to suspect such items will be found, PACEs1(3). (Subsections are included here for clarity; it was not necessary for students to refer to specific subsections when answering.) There were two marks available for the law (AO1).

Application of s1 to Amanda might have started by explaining that she was in a public place – a street – fulfilling this aspect of PACE s1(1). Further application would involve asking (a) whether Brooke was searching for stolen or prohibited items and (b) whether Brooke had reasonable grounds to suspect that Amanda might be carrying such items. Since Brooke searched Amanda due to her annoyance at Amanda pulling a face and making a sneering remark, the search seemed to have been promoted by personal irritation rather than any reasonable grounds for suspecting Amanda was carrying stolen or prohibited items. Furthermore, there was no suggestion that Amanda was carrying stolen or prohibited items, nor that Brooke was looking for such items. We were told that Brooke knew of Amanda’s past activities, but these did not include use of weapons or stealing, and previous convictions, even if there had been any, would not on their own constitute reasonable grounds for suspicion. Since the search did not meet the requirements of PACE s1(2) – (3) it would have been unlawful. There were 3 marks available for application (AO2).

For students who knew the law on stop and search this was a fairly straightforward question. What held some back from gaining full marks was incomplete application. Some merely asserted there were no reasonable grounds to search Amanda without referring to the details in the scenario supporting such an assertion. The best answers referred both to the fact that weapons had never been used by Amanda’s group, and to Brooke’s annoyance at Amanda pulling a face at her. Each of these details was significant. The first allowed students to argue that there were no grounds to suspect Amanda was carrying weapons. The second showed what had actually prompted the search: personal feelings of annoyance, not objective evidence.

Many students showed a very good understanding of the meaning of ‘reasonable’ as requiring an objective basis for the search such as facts, information or intelligence. In the best answers this was then related to Brooke’s apparent personal motivation for the search and the lack of any objective evidence. Some answers also explained that personal factors such as previous convictions could never be sufficient on their own. (Reference to PACE Code A was not required but was, of course, creditworthy.) A minority of answers, however, simply referred to

the police requiring ‘suspicion’ or ‘grounds’ for the search, omitting any reference to the need for an objective basis.

A number of responses confused lawful grounds for arrest with lawful grounds for stop and search, asserting that grounds for a lawful stop and search involved reasonable suspicion that the suspect was committing, or was about to commit, an offence.
71623b-jun25-q-08:
This question required students to advise Emery as to the lawfulness of his arrest, taking into account the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 (PACE) and Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR).

Under s24 PACE a police officer can arrest a person who they have reasonable grounds to suspect is about to commit an offence. Since Emery’s behaviour was creating a risk of injury to others and provoking angry reactions, there would appear to have been reasonable grounds to suspect he was about to commit an offence of bodily harm. The arrest must be necessary for one of the reasons listed in s24(5) which include to prevent the person arrested from causing physical injury to himself or another person. Again, Emery’s behaviour indicated the arrest was necessary for this reason.

The police are a public authority so under s6 of the Human Rights Act 1998 they must act compatibly with the ECHR. Article 5 of the ECHR protects the right to liberty and is intended to guarantee freedom from arbitrary arrest. It thus limits the circumstances in which a person may be deprived of their liberty. To be lawful, any deprivation of liberty must be ‘prescribed by law’ - i.e. have a basis in domestic / national law - and must be for one of the reasons listed. Under 5.1(c) a person may be deprived of their liberty by a lawful arrest, for the purpose of bringing them before the competent legal authority, on reasonable suspicion of having committed an offence, or where it is reasonably considered necessary to prevent them committing an offence.

Applying the provisions of Article 5 to the scenario, Emery’s arrest was ‘prescribed by law’ since it met the requirements of s24 PACE as explained above. Furthermore, it was based on a reasonable suspicion that Emery was about to commit an offence, again as explained above.

 But the scenario stated that the police officer’s main purpose was to protect Emery from being harmed by members of the angry crowd, and they later released him without bringing him before a court. This raises the issue of whether Emery’s arrest was in breach of Article 5 because 5.1 (c) refers to an arrest ‘effected for the purpose of bringing him before the competent legal authority’ and 5.3 states that everyone arrested ‘shall be brought promptly before a judge’. The European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) has held that there must be a degree of flexibility in applying this requirement in order not to unnecessarily prolong a short preventative detention (S v Denmark). In R(Hicks) v Commissioner of Police for the Metropolis the Supreme Court held that preventative detention can be lawful provided the arrest itself was lawful and the detention was for a short period of time only – the ECtHR has indicated this is likely to be hours rather than days (S v Denmark). Here, Emery’s arrest was lawful under PACE s24 as explained above, and Emery was only detained for six hours. If he were to have

been brought before a judge it might have necessitated a longer detention, which would run counter to the aim of Article 5.

So there was a strong argument that Emery’s arrest and detention were lawful, though credit was given for the alternative conclusion.

Some answers dealt only with PACE or only with Article 5.

With regard to PACE, good answers outlined and applied the two requirements for a lawful arrest (reasonable grounds for suspecting an offence was about to be committed, and reasonable grounds to believe the arrest was necessary) while weaker answers often addressed only one of these.

With regard to Article 5, many students were able to explain the concept of a deprivation of liberty, often with reference to a relevant case, and to distinguish it from a mere restriction of movement. Some were then able to confidently identify that an arrest was a deprivation of liberty and then to point out that to comply with Article 5 it had to be prescribed by law and justified under one of the reasons in 5.1(a) – (c).

Some weaker answers showed confusion between a deprivation of liberty and the kettling in Austin v UK, which was held to be a mere restriction of movement. Such students often argued that Emery had not been deprived of his liberty since the six hours he was detained for were less than the period of kettling in Austin.

Many students who identified that there had been a deprivation of liberty went on to argue that it would have been justified under Article 5.1(c) as being reasonably considered necessary to prevent Emery from committing an offence. Other students relied on the 5.1 (b): lawful arrest to secure the fulfilment of an obligation prescribed by law, often relating this to an obligation on the police to take reasonable steps to prevent an imminent breach of the peace. This was also creditworthy. Weaker responses showed uncertainty or confusion over the lawful grounds for a deprivation of liberty.

Some answers referred to the need for an arrest to be a proportionate measure to achieve the aim of preventing the commission of an offence (Ladent v Poland). A strong argument could be made that Emery’s arrest was proportionate to prevent him committing an offence of bodily harm - since his behaviour was creating a danger of falls and injuries to other visitors - and that no less severe measure was available to the police. Weaker responses sometimes referred to wording from the second paragraph of Articles 8, 10 or 11 (i.e. necessary in a democratic society to achieve a legitimate aim).

The requirement that Emery be told the reason for his arrest, under Article 5.2 and PACE s28, was raised by many students, and was given credit.

Some weaker responses simply repeated the facts of the scenario without explaining or applying relevant law from Article 5 or PACE.
71623b-jun25-q-09:
This question had two parts. The first asked students to examine the view that law has an important role to play in balancing conflicting interests. There were 10 marks available for this. The second asked students to discuss the extent to which this balancing role can be seen in the rules protecting a person’s reputation in the context of human rights. There were 5 marks available for this part.

In order to answer the first, non-substantive part of the questions, students could have: • explained the meaning of ‘interest’ and identified different categories of interest, e.g. public/social and private • explained some of the mechanisms by which the law seeks to achieve a balance of interests, especially in substantive law and in rules governing the legal process • explained and analysed areas of law for illustration, identifying the conflicting interests involved and the mechanisms the law uses to achieve a balance between them.

Better answers adopted a broad approach to this part of the question, often starting by identifying different kinds of interests and then examining some of the ideas of philosophers including Bentham, von Jhering, Pound, and Marx. Examples were drawn from a number of areas of substantive law, such as the tort of nuisance, the defence of voluntary intoxication, sentencing or bail.

The best answers examined how the relevant rules of law went about achieving a balance. A commonly used example was the effect of aggravating and mitigating factors on sentencing. The partial nature of the defence of voluntary intoxication was explored in a number of responses. Miller v Jackson was a popular case example, with stronger responses using it to examine the discretionary nature of the remedy of an injunction and why it might be granted or refused to balance the interests of the claimant and defendant. The defence of insanity was also used to examine how the individual interest of a defendant could be balanced against the societal interest in public safety and the victim’s interest in seeing justice done.

Less successful answers often made only a vague reference to the importance of balancing, with no or little attempt to identify the interests that might be in conflict, or how an appropriate balance might actually be achieved.

For the second, substantive part of the question, students needed to first identify the rules of law that protect reputation and then assess the extent to which they balance conflicting interests.

Reputation is an aspect of private life and so falls within Article 8. Since Article 8 is a qualified right, under 8(2) it can be lawfully interfered with to protect the rights and freedoms of others, including the right to freedom of expression, Article 10. In the same way, under 10(2) the right to freedom of expression can be interfered with to protect someone’s reputation. The conflict between these two rights often arises in the context of an action for the tort of misuse of private information where a claimant may wish to prevent the publication of private material which in many cases could affect their reputation. Provided a reasonable expectation of privacy exists, the court will balance the two rights using factors identified in cases such as Axel Springer v Germany, including whether there is a public interest in knowing the information, the previous conduct of the claimant, the consequences of publication for the claimant etc. The tort of defamation specifically protects reputation. The rules set out in the

Defamation Act 2013 attempt to balance protection for reputation with freedom of expression in a number of ways. First, ‘serious harm’ is required (s1) so there is a threshold to reach before someone can sue. Secondly, there are a number of defences which operate to allow freedom of expression if the material is true (s2), or an honest opinion based on fact (s3), or a statement on a matter of public interest (s4).

Some students limited their marks by focusing entirely, or almost entirely, on this second part of the question for which there was a maximum of 5 marks.
71623b-jun25-q-10:
This question required students to apply English law and the ECHR to two distinct, though related, incidents. The first concerned Ivee secretly taking and sharing a photo of her boyfriend, Fynn, and contacting a newspaper with the aim of selling a story about Fynn, his former partner Gina, and her father Hector. The second concerned Fynn being seriously injured after Police failed to take seriously threats to his life from Hector, and the subsequent Police shooting of Kane, who they mistook for Hector.

Photographs have been recognised in a number of cases (such as Von Hannover v Germany (No 2)) as coming within the concept of private life. So Fynn’s private life was interfered with by Ivee secretly taking his photograph and sharing it with Hector. It would be further interfered with if the newspaper published a story about him, Gina and Hector, since information about personal relationships falls clearly within the concept of a private life (recognised in many cases including Pretty v UK). But Ivee was a private individual, not a public authority, so she was not directly bound by s6 of the Human Rights Act 1998 (HRA) to act compatibly with the ECHR. Therefore Fynn could not sue Ivee directly for breach of Article 8.

 Fynn could however bring a claim against Ivee for misuse of private information. This tort requires first that the claimant had a reasonable expectation of privacy in the information at issue – here the photo and the story about Fynn’s bad treatment of Gina, and her father, Hector, threatening Fynn. If a reasonable expectation of privacy is found, the court (which is a public authority under s6 HRA) will then balance the claimant’s right to privacy under Article 8, against the defendant’s right to freedom of expression under Article 10.

Whether or not Fynn had a reasonable expectation of privacy is an objective question. ‘The expectation is that of a reasonable person of ordinary sensibilities placed in the same position as the claimant and faced with the same publicity…’: ZXC v Bloomberg LP. (A very similar wording of the test was set out by the House of Lords in Campbell v MGN Ltd.)

Relevant factors to consider were set out in Murray v Express Newspapers plc: the attributes of the claimant; the nature of the activity in which the claimant was engaged; the place at which it was happening; the nature and purpose of the intrusion; the absence of consent; the effect on the claimant; the circumstances in which and the purposes for which the information came into the hands of the publisher. Photographs are recognised as particularly intrusive (Stoute v News Group Newspapers ltd).

 Applying these Murray factors to the scenario, it would appear that Fynn did have a reasonable expectation of privacy regarding the photograph and the story. Fynn was not famous. The information about his past was shared by Fynn with Ivee in the context of a close personal relationship. Ivee’s purpose was profit. Fynn did not consent to the photograph being taken or shared with Hector, nor to the sharing of the information about his past life with the newspaper. The effect on Fynn of Ivee sending the photograph to Hector was to put his life in danger, and any publication of the story by the newspaper would be very damaging to Fynn and to Gina. Furthermore, Fynn’s bad treatment of Gina had happened twenty years ago and past criminal behaviour is usually regarded as giving rise to a reasonable expectation of privacy (Stoute v News Group Newspapers ltd, par 52, citing Gatley on Libel and Slander, (12 ed)).

Having found that Fynn had a reasonable expectation of privacy, the court would move on to balance Fynn’s Article 8 right with Ivee’s and the newspaper’s Article 10 right. Under s12(4) HRA, where a court is considering whether to grant a remedy (such as an injunction) that would affect the exercise of freedom of expression, the court must have particular regard to the importance of this right. And if the material is journalistic (as the newspaper story would be) the court must have regard to the extent to which the material has, or is about to, become available to the public, and whether publication would be in the public interest. But it is clear from the case law that neither Article 8 nor 10 has precedence and that the balancing has to be carried out with ‘an intense focus’ on the facts of the case (Re S (A Child)). Guidelines for balancing Article 8 and 10 were set out in Axel Springer v Germany and include: whether the information contributes to a debate of general interest; the notoriety of the person concerned and the subject matter of the report; the prior conduct of the person concerned; the method of obtaining the information and its veracity; the content, form and consequences of the publication.

The fact that Fynn’s bad behaviour happened twenty years ago makes it harder to argue there would be a public interest in publishing the story. As noted above, Fynn is not a famous person, nor has he sought the limelight. The photograph was obtained ‘secretly’ without consent and the consequences of publication on Fynn and Gina could be very serious. It is likely therefore that his Article 8 right would outweigh Ivee’s Article 10 right. Fynn could be awarded damages against Ivee for her misuse of his private information and possibly an injunction against the newspaper prohibiting publication of the story.

It was pleasing to see more students aware of the tort of misuse of private information than in previous years, with some able to explain why this would have to be the basis of any claim by Fynn against Ivee. The two-part structure of the tort was not always clear. Some responses went straight to the Axel Springer balancing factors without first considering if there had been a reasonable expectation of privacy. Some students merely asserted that there was an expectation of privacy, but a number of answers outlined and applied the test of a reasonable person of ordinary sensibilities (often citing Campbell). The Murray factors were perhaps less frequently used, but in some answers they were applied very effectively.

Some responses became confused when an attempt was made to apply the terms of 8(2) and 10(2) to Ivee and the newspaper, and Fynn, respectively. This was not necessary. It was certainly creditworthy to point out that each article allows for interference to protect the other. So Article 8(2) allows for a proportionate interference with private life to protect the

rights and freedoms of others (including the right to freedom of expression). Similarly, Article 10(2) allows for proportionate interference with expression to protect the reputation of others, and to prevent the disclosure of information received in confidence. But as part of the tort of misuse of private information, the judge will consider the justifications for interfering with each right, and the proportionality of any interference, at the balancing stage. So there is no need for a separate application of 8(2) or 10(2). Remedies were not always addressed, and when they were many answers revealed confusion over the basis of the claim, often referring to Fynn being awarded damages under s8 HRA, and to Ivee having breached Article 8, rather than Fynn being awarded damages against Ivee for misuse of his private information.

The second part of Q10 concerned possible breaches of Article 2 the right to life and was often more confidently handled than the first part of the question. Most students correctly explained that the police, as agents of the State, were bound under s6 HRA 1998 to act compatibly with the ECHR. And most were able to outline Article 2.1 and to distinguish between the positive duty to protect life (relevant to Fynn) and the negative duty to refrain from taking life (relevant to Kane).

If there is a real and immediate risk to the life of an identified individual, which the police know or ought to know of, they have a duty to take reasonable steps to minimise the risk: Osman v UK. The police were aware of the risk to Fynn’s life from Hector, but did not take the threat seriously. Some students applied the Osman test very effectively, arguing that the risk was both ‘real’ as Hector was a known career criminal, and ‘immediate’ as threats had been made shortly before the hit and run incident. Some students pointed out that reasonable steps might have included investigating the threats or offering Fynn some sort of protection. Since the police had not taken any steps to protect Fynn, most students concluded the police were in breach of their positive duty to protect Fynn’s life. Some students were also able to explain that although Fynn did not die, Article 2 is still engaged if State agents put the victim’s life at serious risk: Makaratzis v Greece. By failing to take any protective action towards Fynn the police had arguably put his life at serious risk. The majority of answers explained that Fynn could sue the police for breach of his Article 2 right under s7 HRA and be awarded an appropriate remedy (damages) under s8.

Some weaker responses lacked the Osman test, simply asserting that the police owed a duty to protect Fynn. Some thought Fynn’s Article 5 right to liberty had been interfered with as he had been forced to leave the UK. Some students elaborated on irrelevant aspects of Article 2, such as when life begins and ends.

The shooting of Kane involved the negative duty on the State not to deprive a person of their life. Article 2.2 sets out situations in which deprivation of life will not be unlawful. To come within one of these exceptions, the force used must be ‘no more than absolutely necessary’ and must be for one of the reasons listed in 2.2(a), (b) or (c). Since the police were trying to arrest Kane, who was pointing a gun at them, the relevant exceptions were 2.2(a) to protect from unlawful violence and 2.2(b) to effect a lawful arrest. Some students elaborated on this by explaining that lethal force has to be strictly proportionate, often citing McCann v UK. Most students argued that given the very serious threat posed by Kane to the police officers (and possibly to other people) shooting him was no more force than absolutely necessary and was strictly proportionate given that Kane had a gun and could open fire on the officers at any

moment. Some students questioned this, pointing out that the officers could perhaps have used a non-lethal shot.

Stronger answers also considered the mistake made by the police in confusing Kane with Hector. Cases such as McCann and Armani da Silva v UK have held that the police using lethal force can rely on an honest mistake which is perceived for good reasons to be valid at the time, but which subsequently turns out to be mistaken. Most students who applied this test concluded that even though Kane was not Hector, the police had good reason to shoot given that he was pointing a gun at them. Some students were able to explain that police operations involving potentially lethal force must be effectively planned and controlled, often citing Finogenov v Russia. Some argued that the mistaking of Kane for Hector pointed to possible errors in planning which, if found, could constitute a breach of Article 2.

Many responses referred to the need for an effective investigation into a death at the hands of State agents, and a number were able to elaborate on what this might entail, e.g. investigation by an independent body, involvement of the next of kin, some element of public scrutiny etc. Jordan v UK was often cited and some students outlined the role of the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC).

Most students concluded that the police were not in breach of Article 2 in relation to the shooting of Kane, and so any action taken against them by Kane’s family for breach of Article 2 would be unsuccessful. A small number of answers also referred to a possible negligence action against the police by Fynn and Kane’s family, with some citing Robinson v Chief Constable of West Yorkshire as authority for the proposition that the police can be sued for negligence if their actions create a reasonably foreseeable risk of harm to a person. It could be argued that if the arrest of a violent career criminal was poorly planned, this would create such a risk.

There were many strong responses to this part of the question, showing a good knowledge of the relevant aspects of Article 2. Some students lost marks by only dealing with one of the victims - Kane or Fynn - but not both.
71623b-jun25-q-11:
The substantive law part of this question concerned two separate examples of protest: the first held outside a zoo, and the second occurring on a later date inside a zoo. Students were asked to apply both English law and the law of the ECHR to the incidents described. Both protests were static and so assemblies, rather than processions. The first involved protestors ‘standing’ on the road outside the zoo holding banners; the second involved Lina and two other protestors shouting at the public from inside the zoo.

The police imposed a limit of 10 on the number that could be present at the first protest outside the zoo. Their power to do this is contained in s14 of the Public Order Act 1986 (POA) and is given to the most senior officer present at the scene. The trigger for imposing conditions is a reasonable belief that conditions are necessary to prevent serious public disorder, or serious damage to property or serious disruption to the life of the community, or that the purpose of the organiser is to intimidate others.

It could be questioned whether the police were justified under s14 POA in imposing a condition on the assembly since there appeared to be no evidence of a risk of serious public disorder or serious disruption to the life of the community. The scenario stated that the protestors did not obstruct the road. Complaints to the police would not seem sufficient grounds to conclude there was a risk of either serious public disorder or serious disruption to the life of the community. An argument could perhaps be made that the protestors’ purpose was to intimidate those going to the zoo. The imposition of the condition limiting numbers would only be lawful if one of the triggers in s14 POA was present.

Many students were aware of the police power to impose conditions under the POA, though the degree of accuracy with which the law was explained varied considerably. In a number of answers there was no explanation and/or application of the triggers for this power and there were few references to the power being given to the senior police officer present at the scene.

A significant number of students referred to the notice requirement in s11 POA 1986. This, however, relates to processions. While organisers of static assemblies might consider it advisable to give the police notice, it is not a legal requirement.

The second protest occurred when Lina and two others climbed over the zoo fence at night and the next morning shouted at the public as they entered. Many students recognised this behaviour as aggravated trespass under s68 of the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994 (CJPOA). The strongest responses defined aggravated trespass as requiring trespass and some form of disruption or obstruction or intimidation. Applying this to the scenario it was clear that Lina and the other two members of the group had trespassed on to private property when they climbed over the zoo fence. By shouting at the public they were arguably disrupting and/or obstructing the lawful activity of visiting the zoo and/or intimidating the public from visiting the zoo. This was reinforced by the mention in the scenario of children becoming upset.

Under s69 CJPOA a police officer can ask a person reasonably believed to be committing aggravated trespass to leave. Failure to comply is an offence for which the police officer can then arrest the person concerned. So the arrest of Lina after she refused to leave the zoo was lawful under s69 CJPOA.

While some students recognised the aggravated trespass, not all who did were able to define it or point to the source of law for this offence. Some students applied the law on trespassory assembly from s14A POA. While some credit was given for this, a trespassory assembly is a gathering of 20 or more people whereas there were only three protestors inside the zoo. Some students referred to s61 CJPOA giving police the power to remove trespassers who have an intention to reside on land, but Lina and the other two protestors did not have such a purpose.

The behaviour inside the zoo could also be considered a breach of the peace, defined in R v Howell as where harm is done or threatened to be done to a person or in their presence to their property, or when a person is put in fear of such harm. Some students pointed out that breach of the peace could apply both to the protestors and the members of the public who

were throwing stones. Stronger answers went on to explain that a police officer has a duty to take reasonable steps, including arrest, to deal with a breach of the peace or to prevent a breach of the peace reasonably believed to be imminent. The police first asked Lina to leave and then, when she refused, arrested her. Since Lina and the other two group members were trespassing and provoking angry reactions from the public, these steps were arguably reasonable ways to deal with the breach of the peace, whether considered actual or imminent.

Many students explained that the police, as agents of the State, are bound to act compatibly with the ECHR under s 6 HRA 1998. Most students recognised the relevance of Article 11 to the incidents in the scenario, though not all saw the relevance of Article 10.

The right under Article 11 is a right to ‘peaceful’ assembly. Since the scenario stated that there was no obstruction of traffic by the protestors on the roadside, most students concluded that this assembly was peaceful. Some went on to point out that a peaceful assembly can nevertheless be lawfully interfered with in certain circumstances, often citing Cisse v France.

The protestors were also exercising their right to freedom of expression by carrying banners saying ‘Zoos are prisons’. In some answers the Article 10 right was only considered when discussing the second protest in which protestors shouted from inside the zoo, but the banners held by the protestors in the first protest outside the zoo were clearly a form of expression.

These two articles are closely linked since the aim of a protest is to express a view or opinion. Many students pointed out that both protest and expression can shock or disturb and yet still fall within Articles 11 and 10, often citing Ollinger v Austria and/or Handyside v UK.

The condition limiting the number at the roadside assembly to 10, the later instruction to Lina and the other two group members to leave the zoo, and Lina’s subsequent arrest were all interferences by the police with the protestors’ rights to freedom of assembly and association under Article 11 and to freedom of expression under Article 10. But since Articles 10 and 11 are qualified rights, they can lawfully be interfered with under 10(2) or 11(2) if the interference is prescribed by law and necessary in a democratic society in pursuit of one of the listed aims. In stronger responses each of the above interferences with Article 10 and 11 was identified and checked against these criteria.

Prescribed by law means having a basis in domestic law. Some students elaborated on this, explaining the law must be clear and accessible. In the scenario, the imposition of the condition limiting numbers was prescribed by the POA. The instruction to Lina and the other two group members to leave, and the subsequent arrest of Lina were prescribed by law under the CJPOA s68-69, and the common law on breach of the peace.

‘Necessary in a democratic society’ means that the interference must correspond to a pressing social need and be a proportionate measure to achieve a legitimate aim (Handyside v UK). Aims relevant to the scenario were public safety and the prevention of disorder and crime. Some students examined the proportionality of the limit on numbers by asking if it was the least intrusive means to achieve these aims. In some responses it was argued that the limit on

numbers to 10 was not a proportionate measure given that the protest was not obstructing traffic. Weaker responses failed to apply the proportionality principle at all.

If the limit on numbers was found to be disproportionate then this interference would have been in breach of Articles 10 and 11, entitling protestors to take action under s7 HRA and allowing the awarding of an appropriate remedy under s8 HRA.

With regard to the police asking the protestors inside the zoo to leave and the arrest of Lina, there was a much stronger argument that these steps were proportionate to the legitimate aims of public safety, and preventing disorder and crime. The presence of the protestors was clearly upsetting both adults and children and seemed likely to lead to violence as adult members of the public were shouting back at them and throwing stones. Furthermore, the protestors were trespassing and many students recognised that while Article 11 protects protest on public land, the same is not generally true for private property, often citing Appelby v UK. So it could be argued there was no protection from Article 11 here.

Some students pointed out that the behaviour of the public (shouting back and throwing stones) was similar to a counter protest. Many students were aware that the State has a positive duty to police protests so as to protect peaceful protestors from violent counter protests. Cases such as Ezelin v France and Platform Artze fur das Leben v Austria were often cited in support of this. On this basis it was argued that there was a possible breach of Article 11 due to the police’s failure to protect Lina and the other two group members from the public. However, as some students recognised, this argument was unlikely to succeed because Lina and her two companions were trespassing and so no longer exercising their right to peaceful protest.

The last part of Q11 asked students to assess the contribution of different sources of law to the rules they had explained and applied to the scenario. This non-substantive aspect was worth 7 marks.

The relevant sources of law were common law, statute and the ECHR. To gain full marks on this part, students needed to briefly explain each source and then give an example from their answer.

Common law is law made by judges when deciding cases. An example could be the law on breach of the peace which was defined in R v Howell. This was relevant to the behaviour inside the zoo (shouting and stone throwing).

Statutory law, or legislation, is law made by Parliament. Examples of such law applied to the scenario would be the POA and the CJPOA. The POA sets out the law allowing conditions to be imposed on assemblies. This was relevant to the police imposing a limit of 10 on the number allowed at the roadside protest. The CJPOA defines the offence of aggravated trespass which was applicable to Lina and the two members of the group who climbed over the fence to get into the zoo and then shouted at the public.

The ECHR is an international treaty setting out rights such as freedom of expression and freedom of assembly and association in Articles 10 and 11 respectively. These rights were being exercised by the protestors. The police, as agents of the State, are bound to act compatibly with these rights under s6 HRA. So to be lawful the actions of the police in dealing with incidents had to fall within the terms of 10(2) and 11(2).

There were some thoughtful responses to this part of the question, though not many addressed all three sources. Not all students understood what ‘sources of law’ referred to. Some students limited their marks by failing to link the sources they had identified to any law applied to the scenario. In a number of responses there was confusion between the ECHR and European Union law. In some of these answers, directives and regulations were discussed, for which there was no credit.
